I understand
that we have passed all the items embodied in this resolution and it now merely remains to consider the resolution as a whole. In the course of the discussion of the various items the hon. member (Mr. Cahan) and I both asked that the minister provide, in relation to the items affected by the West India treaty, that those items should1 come into effect only upon the ratification of that treaty. We urged that they be left in abeyance until such time as action one way or the other might be taken upon the treaty. The minister declared that he was following precedent in the course he proposed to take. I admit that he will find precedent for that course, but I assure him that he will not find any precedent for a situation analogous to the present. Under the former treaty with the West Indies, so far as I know, no damage was done to any Canadian industry, and everyone was in favour of the treaty. To-day the claim is seriously put forward that Canadian industry will suffer as a result of the tariff it is proposed to enact in relation to the West India treaty. At the moment I am referring particularly to the increase in duties on cocoa beans, and in order that my objection may be stated as concisely- as possible, I am going to read a letter which I have received from one of the manufacturers. The minister, I think, is perfectly familiar with the circumstances:
When the West Indies treaty is ratified we will have to pay two cents per pound duty on foreign grown cocoa beans, one and a half cents per pound on British grown cocoa beans, exclusive of West Indies kinds, and West Indies kinds wiW come in free.
We will not be able to use cocoa beans grown in the West Indies, except in very limited quantities. The price of Trinidad cocoa beans is always several cents per pound higher than Accra cocoa beans which are grown in British West Africa. We will, therefore, continue to bring in Accra cocoa beans, and will have to pay the duty of one and a half cents per pound on them. Cocoa beans from Jamaica we cannot use except in very limited quantities, because of their poor quality.
I pause here to ask the minister whether there is anything in the foregoing statement of fact with which he disagrees. I do not think there is; the minister does not reply. So that we have no issue on the question of fact that the manufacturers will now have to pay a duty of one and a hail-f cents per pound on the cocoa beans which they import from British West Africa; nor is the fact denied

that they will be unable to use the beans which will come in from the West Indies. The writer continues:
On from 80 to 85 per cent of the cocoa beans we will use, we will be forced to ipay a duty of one and a half cents per pound or tiwo cents per pound. Now, from 100 pounds of cocoa beans we only gat from seventy-five to eighty pounds of cleaned cocoa beans.
He goes on to indicate what the effect will be on the trade. We have had the discussion as to whether this tariff should be enacted or not, and all I intend to do now is to ask the minister to assure the committee that these duties will not be put into effect until the West India treaty becomes operative.

Suppose we
take these resolutions section by section?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
On section 1.
Listening to what the chairman has read, apparently drop letters and postcards are still to be subject to two cents postage?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Then what is
the reason for introducing this at all? What is the change?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, becoming
effective on July 1, the rate of postage on all letters will foe two cents instead of three. The postage on drop letters wild remain the same as heretofore. Let me read the notation :
This section will remove (the one cent additional postage on letters for transmission by post for any distance within Canada; the additional cent wilj remain on drop letters and post cards as heretofore; effective July 1, 1926. The estimated reduction in taxation for (the nine months wild be $4,125,000; for the twelve months $5,500,000.

Mr. Chairman, it does seem to me that the minister by his explanation has not unravelled this Chinese puzzle. I recall that Talleyrand once wittily said, "Language was given us to conceal our thoughts." I think if a serious effort had been made to give effect to that purpose it could not have been more successfully served than by this clause. If the intention of the government is to make the rate of postage two cents on letters dropped, we will say, in the city of Ottawa for delivery outside of Ottawa, why is it not possible to say so in plain, understandable language? I understand that the intention of the minister, and the effect of this clause, is to retain the rate of postage on local letters; for example, on a letter dropped in the post office here for delivery at a residence within the city the rate of postage will continue to be two cents, instead of reverting to the pre-war rate of one cent on such letters. But I do press upon the minister the desirability of so recasting this clause that a mind less dense than mine may be able to understand it.

Mr. Chairman, this impost is nothing but a nuisance tax in a new form and causes the utmost trouble to the public. It is going to cause untold annoyance just at a time when business men are congratulating themselves that some of these burdens and nuisances are being eliminated. I venture

Special War Revenue Act
to say that the people will not use the post card in this form, and that we will get far less revenue than was formerly received. The city of Toronto contributes $6,000,000 yearly to the postal revenues of the country, yet we cannot get an up-to-date post office. With the many amendments to the Postal Act we already have great difficulty in knowing what the law is, and now, when the government say they are reducing taxes and eliminating nuisance taxes, they impose a regulation of this kind which it requires a lawyer to understand. I urge the minister to consider the advice of the heads of the postal service, because this is nothing but a new form of nuisance tax which will place barriers in the way of business in this country. In the larger cities there are many foreigners; who is to explain this amendment to them, and to the people in the rural places as well?
The time has come when the post office should be placed on a proper basis. It is very unfortunate that we have no Postmaster General in the House. From 1899 to the beginning of the wrar we had a surplus from the post office, and all the various postmasters general tried to cater to the public, and give them the proper facilities desired. But now when everyone is hoping for a revival of trade this obnoxious, objectionable regulation is brought forward, which means nothing and which will take a good deal of revenue from the government. I would like the minister to tell us who recommended this change, whether the heads of the postal service have been consulted; what revenue will come out of it and how it will help trade in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Apparently the hon. member
for Mount Royal (Mr. White) misunderstood the reading of the clause. This legislation was drafted to meet the wishes of the Post Office department, who administer the act. They understand it quite well.
What about the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And the public understand it.
To show that the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) has not read the clause, he finds fault because the revenue is to be reduced. Certainly it is to be reduced; that is the intention. It is going to lighten the taxes of the people who are doing business. It is quite true that the postage on a drop letter will be the same as that on a letter going to any other part of Canada, but the Post Office Department estimate that, with the requirements of the cities for delivery at each house, it costs just as much to deliver these letters as to send a letter uoil-237|
from Ottawa to Vancouver. So the postage is made uniform, two cents on drop letters and post cards, as before.

My hon. friend interests me very much. He tells us that it costs just as much to look after a drop letter, because there is local delivery here, as to send a letter from Ottawa to Vancouver. I was under the impression that Vancouver also had a local delivery, and that this was general in all cities and towns. I was further under the impression that we have rural mail delivery to-day, which is very expensive, in a large part of the country. I am afraid my hon. friend's brief is not right; I think the Post Office Department has loaded him wrongly there. Certainly the illustration they give is very wide of the mark. Could my hon. friend really tell us why the post office think the reduction should be made in this way; whether it is because they think it will cost the treasury far less than if they were to reduce drop letters and post cards to one cent? Is that not the real reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, my hon. friend is quite
right; had we been in a position to lose $2,000,000 more we could have gone back to the conditions prevailing prior to 1915. But under this plan we figure that we will lose $5,500,000 during the year, and that is all we can afford.
The whole thing really amounts to this; the drop letters and post cards are not looked after because the government cannot afford to go further than they have gone?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I have one strong objection.
If it is the theory of the government that the one cent on drop letters and post cards is not enough, why add the extra cent as a tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend fails to understand the regulation. We are adding nothing, but simply amending the legislation of 1915 and removing the extra cent from the letters. We are not removing it from drop letters and post cards.

But the proposed regulation
reads as follows:
On every post card for transmission by post for any distance within Canada and on every letter and post card posted at and intended for delivery through the same post office, there shall be levied and collected a tax of 1 cent-
The effect in the end is the same; on a post card or drop letter you pay your postage of one cent and this extra tax of one cent, which tax is not paid on a letter going
Special War Revenue Act

from here to Vancouver or to anywhere else in Canada. The result is that you draw a tax distinction between drop letters and post cards and other letters than drop letters. Why can you not amend the Postal Act and raise the rate of postage, rather than do this by way of an extra tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is not in the form of
an extra tax; we are repealing certain parts of the legislation of 1915, the Special War Revenue Act. My hon. friend has paid the postage which he now complains of since April 15, 1915, and we are relieving him of this postage on letters.

I am not complaining of
anything in the way of paying. The net result is exactly the same. But I do say this: While you are making this change you are making it in a wrong way. You say that you are not imposing anything. I say that this does impose expressly a substantial tax of one cent. It is there already, I know, but you are removing the tax from the long distance letter and the net result is that you are leaving a one cent tax on post cards and drop letters, while you are taking the cent tax olf the long distance letter. You are doing expressly what I said a moment ago: You are making a tax distinction between the post cards and drop letters and the long distance letters ,and the thing is wrong. If you are not satisfied with your postage, alter the rate of it.

It is enoouraging
the long haul.

I should like to point out
the objection I have to this resolution. The tax of an extra cent should be passed on to those best able to pay it. I would ask the minister to consider this question of the ability of the working classes, the farmers, and the ordinary people of this country who use post cards, to pay this added cent. Does the minister know that to-day the government of Canada is practically giving the newspapers of this country a bonus of $8,000,000 in the carriage of the newspapers? That is according to the returns I got in the House of Commons last session. The newspapers are carried as third-class matter, and it cost the government to carry these newspapers $8,000,000 more than they received in revenue for the service. So that the post office is practically giving to the newspapers of Canada a bonus or subsidy of $8,000,000. The newspapers of this country are carried practically free, as third-class mail. If you can do that for some of these rich corporations owning newspapers in this country, corporations strong enough sometimes to control parliament and

nominate political leaders, surely you can do something for the poor workingman who has to pay this extra cent on post cards. This tax is unfair to the large centres of population, which are now bearing the greater proportion of the cost of administration of the post office. The revenue of the post office comes largely from the large cities of Canada. Toronto's contribution, $6,000,000, is equal to the contributions of the cities of Hamilton, Montreal, Halifax, Winnipeg and Vancouver put together. I think the working class in the large centres should have the benefit of one cent postage on post cards. To-day they have to pay one cent, plus this additional cent, or two cents to have a post card delivered in their own city, and this tax will largely be taken from the large centres like Toronto, to maintain public utilities here and there in different parts of the country. It is class legislation of the worst kind. There is one class of legislation for the newspapers and large corporations, and a different class of legislation for the working classes. A post card posted in Parkdale, for instance, to be delivered across the road will have to pay a tax of two cents. I say that is class legislation of the worst kind. Furthermore, the returns of the Postmaster General show that the more restrictions you put on mail, the more nuisance taxes you impose upon it, the less revenue you get. That is a well known principle in the administration of the post office. When you remove the nuisance taxes, automatically you increase the number of users of that form of communication. Impose restrictions on that class of mail, and automatically fewer people use that particular form of communication.
What we need, Mir. Chairman, is a Postmaster general sitting in this House, not an Acting Postmaster General. I have every confidence in the ability of the present Acting Postmaster General, the Minister 4 p.m. of Justice, who is very popular, but he has enough to do to look after his own department; he is almost a quorum of the cabinet in himself. What does the British Postmaster iGeneral do when he has a surplus? He hands it back to the people who use the mails, by lessening the charges and giving them increased facilities. In England the radio, the telephone and everything else are connected to-day with the British post office, which is doing everything it can to encourage a revival of trade and commerce. But what are you doing in this country? At this late hour of the day you are imposing restrictions which will retard the use of this particular form of communication. What part of the revenue derived from this tax will

Special War Revenue Act
be used to provide proper postal facilities in the city of Toronto? The revenue Toronto contributes will be used to maintain post offices in other parts of the country. We want a proper postal service, and at the present time we have not got proper postal facilities in the city of Toronto. Now the minister comes along and imposes restrictions on the use of post cards within the four comers and gates of that city. I do not think the public will stand for it.

I am somewhat
surprised that the Minister of Finance has not put up the usual reason for this change, namely, that this is another endeavour to keep the boys and girls on the farm. That was the usual justification for changes made in the past. In 1915, whatever tax was put on as a special war revenue tax, it was evenly distributed; it was a fair and just tax. This tax is a discriminatory tax and nothing else. There is not a fair distribution of the tax; it is a tax upon the cities. I suppose the minister forgot his usual reason to justify this change, that it was for the purpose of keeping the boys and girls on the farm.

What is the
annual deficit each year on the rural mail delivery service?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not got that.

Then it is all
nonsense to say it costs as much to deliver a letter from one side of the street to another in Toronto as it does to deliver it in Vancouver. The minister should know what the deficit is before making such a statement.

I agree entirely with the
observations that have been made with respect to discrimination. I would like to ask the minister a question with reference to the postage on letters going to the United States. Has the minister considered the advisability of increasing: the postal rates on newspapers? What is the present rate on newspapers?

speechtext:

The men who run the newspapers, particularly some of the newspapers that strongly supported my hon. friend in the last election, do not adopt that point of view. They have represented to the government very strongly that we should reduce the charges for carrying newspapers. We will look into your case, but you are sending advertising matter through the mail throughout Canada, and you have a right to pay for it." I want to be frank and say they are not all taking that attitude.

Name them.
Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not like to name any of them, but there are newspapers which have been very decent toward my hon. friend from Toronto Northwest, and which argue that the newspapers should be carried for less. The government does not share that view.

I can tell the
minister-and he knows it-that we are carrying newspapers for less than cost. We are carrying newspapers on express trains, taking them in bulk to-day, at a less figure than the ordinary freight rate. Further than that, Mr. Chairman, the minister says that the big newspapers, some of those that are helping their party, are in favour of it. How about the newspapers which are helping the other side?
Not very many.

I do not care
what side they are on, they are entitled to pay their share for the delivery of their own goods. That is the stand I took in this House when we changed the rates a few years .ago, and I do not think the minister is doing himself justice when he tries to make out that we on this side of the House are not prepared to tackle the question. Evidently he is not prepared to touch it. The rate given to the newspapers to-day is below cost, and what is happening is this: Under the present system the minister is helping to put the small country newspapers out of business. Today they are delivering some of these large newspapers at a less rate than is granted to the ordinary country newspaper. I venture to say that a large number of newspapers, I I was going to say a thousand, have gone out of business. Certainly quite a large number have ceased operations due to the action of this parliament.
I will agree that newspapers are being carried at a very low rate, but I rise to a point of order. This provision deals with the method of taxation.

I did not fully catch the
reply of the minister in reference to the rate to the United Kingdom. The present rate to the United States and to points in Canada is three cents and the rate to the United Kingdom is four cents. Is it not contemplated by the government to make a proportionate reduction in the rate of postage to the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have to sumbit that to the post office authorities.
It is not in this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not in this bill.
It is not in the budget.

I submit
to the House in all seriousness that the drafting of this clause is as clear as mud. Look at it. It says:
-there shaiLl be levied and collected a tax of one cent in addition to postage payable in the form of a postage stamp to be affixed thereto at or before the time of posting the letter or post card; but such tax shall not be levied or collected on any letter or post card.
The tax of one cent is distinct and separate, according to the phraseology of this paragraph, from the postage stamp. Why not say in clear easy and comprehensive language that the rate of postage on a certain class of letter shall, after the first of July be two cents? Why not repeal this section, entirely, remove it from the war revenue, and amend your Post Office Act with a very simple and short three or four line section, so that he who runs may read? I know what the minister intends and what the department intends, but the man who, unaware of the intention of the government, undertakes to obtain this information from this paragraph will land himself in an insane asylum before he understands it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He has bad ten years to get there, because we are following exactly the language of my hon. friend's name-sake who introduced this legislation in 1915, and it was approved by the Department of Justice.
Mr. (NEILL:	I suggest that we hold this

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not involved in this
legislation at all.

given as a receipt.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have a memorandum which reads as follows:
This is for the purpose of removing doubt as to whether goods are liable to sales tax when sold under process of law or under a lien. The court of appeal of the province of Quebec in the case of the King versus the Bank of Hochelaga by unanimous decision has ruled that a bank is not required to pay the sales tax on the sale of a stock in trade sold by them in pursuance of a security obtained under section 88 of the Bank Act. Quite sometime ago the Macamic Pulp and Paper Company made an assignment under the Bankruptcy Act and the Bank of Hochelaga,-now the Ban-que Canadienne Nationale,-seized and sold the company's stock in pursuance of a security which they held under section 88 of the Bank Act. The department therefore requested the bank to pay a tax on the sale of that stock on the ground that when a bank assumes the status of a manufacturer or producer and sells a stock which in the ordinary course would have been subject to the sales tax, they should be required to assume the same liability as any ordinary manufacturer or producer so far as the sales tax is concerned. Our view in the matter was upheld by a ruling made by the Department of Justice in April 1923 and I understand that the banks have always been paying the sales tax when realizing under their securities. In this particular case, however, the Bank of Hochelaga refused to pay the tax and the matter had, therefore, to be submitted to the courts for decision. The Superior Court of Montreal gave a decision in favour of the bank which decision was subsequently upheld by the appeal court of the province. In the circumstances I would suggest that section 19 BBB of the Special War Revenue Act be amended so as to provide that in future all sales of stock seized by a bank or any other pledgee or lien holder be subject to the sales tax just as if the goods were sold by the manufacturer or produces* himself.
This is signed by Noel Chasse, departmental solicitor.

We are not clarifying the law; we are changing it. The law we take from the courts. We are told by the unanimous decision of the court of appeal of Quebec that the sales tax under these circumstances is not collectable. I do not know that it is right that it should not be collectable; but let us be fair with ourselves. We are changing the law and providing for more sales tax under these circumstances. I do not see any reason why the tax should not be paid by these people.

My view of the matter is that where a company's stock is seized by a creditor it is a hardship on both the creditor and the company for the government to come

in and take out a tax in the form of a sales tax. If a sale has been effected under those circumstances surely there is no need for the government to extend a tax that is vicious in any case. I never heard anybody on general principles support the sales tax; it is in force only of necessity as a war measure. You are going rather far. Where there is seizure and sale under legal proceedings the creditor in nine cases out of ten does not get the whole of his money. I think yod might very well leave the sales tax as it stands instead of extending it to cases where undoubtedly there will be a hardship.

Is there not a danger under this section of 'goods having to pay the sales tax twice? Take the case of manufactured goods in the hands of a trader. On those goods the sales tax has already been paid by the manufacturer, and under this section I can see a great probabilty of their having to pay the tax a second time. I do not conceive that to be the intention of the provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under the present law the
sales tax is collected only once. This provision applies to goods on which the sales tax has not yet been collected and which may have been taken over by a bank. On such goods the government has a right to its charges.
How many articles are exempt from the sales tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a long list of them.
The minister says the government is entitled to the sales tax on such goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just as a law court is entitled to the charges which it levies.

Surely the basis of that contention must be that there is some profit out of which to get the sales tax; but in many cases of seizure there will be no profit and the government will simply be taking the tax out of the pocket of the creditor. That is entirely wrong. If you could prove that there was some profit accruing there might be something to be said for exacting the tax, but there is no justification whatever either in law or in reason for the government to collect the tax out of the pocket of the already suffering creditor who most probably, in any event, will not get the whole of his money.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The creditor has nothing to
do with it.

Why not?

Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Ever since the sales tax has
been under discussion all the arguments on both sides of the House have gone to prove that the consumer pays the tax.

If goods are seized under
process of law and are put up for sale by the sheriff, there is no knowing who pays the tax. But it is a safe assumption that in nine cases out of ten it will be the unfortunate creditor who will foot the bill, for he will get so much less. The government is therefore taking the tax out of his pocket.
I care not what has been said in previous parliaments; I have my own sins to bear, and so far as I am concerned the whole principle is pernicious.

My hon. friend's sins are light. It seems to me that when it comes to a question of principle it is rather difficult to defend any tax which you do not want to pay. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) no doubt knows, we have in the Bank Act a provision whereby banks may make advances in connection; with manufacturing processes and similar enterprises on which they have a very effective lien. Some people contend that this provision should not be retained in the act, but it is a part of our banking system. That lien enhances the bank's position, which is already one of considerable advantage as against everyone else. The bank taking action, the courts of the province of Quebec, at least, have held that it need not pay the tax. We are here really dealing altogether with the banks, and clearly the bank is in a unique position: it may, and as a matter of fact it does in many instances, virtually carry on the business. Now I do not like the tax any more than dioes my hon. friend (Mr. Bury), but in the matter of taxation we must try to deal fairly with all; we should not help one trader as against another. We must try to preserve an equality of taxation among the people from whom we secure revenues, and we cannot do so if the bank, with special privileges, can force the sale of goods without paying anything in the way of fealee tax, while interest must be paid to the bank. That is the feature that appeals to me.

If a bank, having a lien on
certain stock, steps into the shoes of the proprietor and carries on the business it should pay the sales tax. But I am not dealing with such a case. I am suggesting the case of a seizure of goods made by a lien holder and the subsequent sale by the sheriff under proceedings similar to those taken under a writ
of fieri facias. I have not in mind either the case of a bank, such as my hon. friend has mentioned, or the case of a receivership; I am not discussing anything of that nature. I am referring exclusively to cases of seizure by a sheriff under a lien note or a chattel mortgage or a writ of execution. In nine cases out of ten the creditor fails to realize the full amount owing to him and the government proposes now to scoop the sales tax out of the proceeds he receives. If there were any margin of profit over and above the taxable costs of the debt due to the creditor then I would say that the government might be entitled to the sales tax out of that surplus. But I cannot see how the government can fairly assert a preferred claim in respect of the sales tax. It is just that sort of thing that is hurting us in Alberta. I do not know how far it is true of this government, but in that province the government has persistently pressed, in front of the secured creditor, government charge after government charge until the secured creditor does not know where he is. The result is that loans are not made. The principle is a pernicious one, and if the minister would consider the advisability of confining the sales tax to cases in judicial proceedings where there is some margin over and above the just debt, the difficulty might be got over. Where, on the other hand, as my hon. friend has mentioned, the lien holder exercising his rights steps into the shoes of the proprietor and continues in business, then as a trader he is certainly under a moral obligation to pay the sales tax. But that is vastly different from the realization of the whole capital stock at once under a sheriff's sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This will apply only to such goods as are liable to the sales tax in the first instance, and there is a great list of exemptions. At once I start with a 5 per cent advantage over him. He will see that we must be fair to all traders. That is the reason for this legislation.

The hon. minister has not met my objection at all. I am talking of realization under a sheriff's sale, where the articles are sold in gross and where there is no possible competition with the other man down the street who is selling the same kind of goods. I stated expressly that I was not citing the case of a creditor exercising his right of lien and selling over the counter the
Special War Revenue Act

stock of goods in the store. In that case undoubtedly he is in the shoes of the trader and he will have to shoulder the burden of the trader in the form of sales tax. But suppose I have a chattel mortgage on the stock in trade of the trader who has not yet paid his sales tax, and who would have had to pay it if the goods were sold in the ordinary way in the course of business over the counter. If the sheriff seizes those goods under my chattel mortgage-as he would do in Alberta- and advertises them en bloc by auction on a certain day, do you mean to tell me there is any question of competition in such a case? There is no competition at all, for the prices paid at an auction of that kind will not be anything like the prices paid on the same goods sold at retail over the counter in the ordinary course of business.

Mr. Chairman, under this item I wanted to bring a matter to the attention of the minister which I cannot gee any way of doing otherwise. Under the law a great many manufacturers are being made to pay the sales tax twice, once upon the equipment and again upon the goods therewith produced. Their competitors pay no such tax; you do not reach any of them in the United States, England or anywhere else with that tax. In short, you are putting a direct double tax upon the Canadian manufacturer. I do not know why it was done; I do not know how much the minister makes out of this tax, and I should like to get some information about it. It was first done in 1924.
